source_refs.note: Chapter 3 exercise (PDF 71-74, printed 68-71), solved: MCQ keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints none), model answers for the short, constructed response and comprehensive questions, and step-by-step numerical solutions checked against the printed answers.

blocks.prompt: 3.1 The ratio of angular speed of minute's hand and hour's hand of watch is:
blocks.explanation: The minute hand makes one revolution in 60 min and the hour hand in 12 h = 720 min. ω = 2π/T, so ω(minute) : ω(hour) = 720 : 60 = 12 : 1.

blocks.prompt: 3.2 A body travelling in a circle at constant speed:
blocks.explanation: Its speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes at every point, so it has a centripetal acceleration a = v²/r directed towards the centre (3.2).

blocks.prompt: 3.3 A stone at the end of long string is whirled in vertical circle at a constant speed. The tension in the string will be minimum when the stone is:

options.text: at the top of the circle

blocks.explanation: At the top, weight mg and tension T both point towards the centre: T + mg = mv²/r, so T = mv²/r − mg (minimum). At the bottom T = mv²/r + mg (maximum).

blocks.prompt: 3.4 Every point of rotating rigid body has:
blocks.explanation: All points of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis have the same angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration; their linear velocity v = rω depends on r (3.1).

blocks.prompt: 3.5 The minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into the orbit is called:
blocks.explanation: v = √(gR) = 7.9 km s⁻¹ is the minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into the orbit, called the critical velocity (3.3).

blocks.prompt: 3.6 An astronaut is orbiting around the Earth in a large capsule. Then,

options.text: he will be in a state of weightlessness with respect to capsule
he is freely falling towards the Earth
a ball projected at an angle has a straight line path as observed by him

blocks.explanation: The capsule and the astronaut both fall freely towards the Earth with the same acceleration g, so the supporting force is zero (weightlessness). Relative to the capsule nothing falls, so a projected ball moves in a straight line as seen by him. All three are true.

blocks.prompt: 3.7 An object in uniform circular motion makes 10 revolutions in 2 seconds. Which of the following statement is true?
blocks.explanation: f = 10 rev ÷ 2 s = 5 Hz, and T = 1/f = 0.2 s.

blocks.prompt: 3.8 A man inside the artificial satellite feels weightlessness because the force of attraction due to the Earth is:

options.text: balanced by the force of attraction due to the moon
non-effective due to some particular design of the satellite

blocks.explanation: The whole gravitational pull mg is used up as the centripetal force mv²/r, so mg = mg − F_N gives F_N = 0 (3.3).

blocks.prompt: 3.9 A bottle of soda water is grasped from the neck and swung briskly in a vertical circle. Near which portion of the bottle do the bubbles collect?

options.text: Bubbles remain distributed throughout the volume of the bottle.
Near the neck of the bottle

blocks.explanation: The neck is near the axis of rotation. As in a centrifuge, the denser liquid goes outward (to the bottom of the bottle) and the lighter gas bubbles collect near the axis, i.e. near the neck (3.2).

blocks.prompt: 3.10 The moment of inertia of body depends upon:

options.text: mass of the body and its distribution about axis of rotation

blocks.explanation: I = Σ mᵢrᵢ²: it depends on the mass and on how the mass is distributed about the axis of rotation (3.4).

blocks.prompt: 3.1 State second law of motion in case of rotation.
blocks.explanation:
The torque acting on a rotating rigid body is equal to the product of its moment of inertia and angular acceleration: τ = Iα.
It is the rotational analogue of F = ma (F → τ, m → I, a → α).

blocks.prompt: 3.2 What is the effect of changing the position of a diver while diving in the pool?
blocks.explanation:
By curling his arms and legs in, the diver decreases his moment of inertia, so his angular velocity increases (Iω = constant) and he makes more somersaults.
By stretching out before entering the water he increases I, so ω decreases and he enters the water smoothly.

blocks.prompt: 3.3 How do we get butter from the milk?
blocks.explanation: Milk is whirled rapidly in a cream separator (or churned). Milk is a mixture of light and heavy particles: the lighter fat (cream) particles gather near the axis of rotation and the heavier particles move outward. The cream collected near the axis is taken out and churned into butter.

blocks.prompt: 3.4 Mass is a measure of inertia in linear motion. What is its analogue in rotational motion? Describe briefly.
blocks.explanation:
Moment of inertia (I) is the rotational analogue of mass. It measures the resistance of a body to a change in its rotational motion.
I = Σ mᵢrᵢ²; it depends on the mass and its distribution about the axis of rotation. Unit: kg m².

blocks.prompt: 3.5 Why is it harder for a car to take turn at higher speed than at lower speed?
blocks.explanation: The centripetal force needed for a turn is F = mv²/r, which grows as v². On a level road this force comes from friction between the tyres and the road, which is limited. At high speed the required force becomes more than the friction can give, so the car skids outward.

blocks.prompt: 3.6 What are the benefits of using rare wheels of heavy vehicles consisted of double tires?
blocks.explanation:
Double tyres share the heavy load, so each tyre carries less weight and the pressure on the road is less.
The larger contact area gives more grip (friction), which provides the needed centripetal force on turns and gives stability; if one tyre bursts the other still supports the vehicle.

blocks.prompt: 3.7 When a moving car turns around a corner to the left, in what direction do the occupants tend to fall? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation:
They tend to fall to the right (outward from the turn).
Due to inertia their bodies tend to keep moving in a straight line while the car turns left; the seat and friction must supply the centripetal force to turn them with the car.

blocks.prompt: 3.8 Why is the acceleration of a body moving uniformly in a circle, directed towards the centre?
blocks.explanation: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant and only the direction of velocity changes. The change in velocity (Δv) at every point is along the radius towards the centre, so the acceleration a = v²/r (and the centripetal force producing it) is directed towards the centre.

blocks.prompt: 3.9 How does an astronaut feel weightlessness while orbiting from the Earth in a space-ship?
blocks.explanation:
The space-ship and the astronaut both fall freely towards the Earth with the same acceleration g; the Earth's pull provides only the centripetal force.
So mv²/r = mg − F_N gives F_N = 0: the floor exerts no supporting force on him, and he feels weightless.

blocks.prompt: 3.1 If angular velocity of different particles of a rigid body is constant, will the linear velocity of these particles also constant?
blocks.explanation:
No. All particles of a rotating rigid body have the same angular velocity ω, but their linear velocity is v = rω.
Particles farther from the axis (larger r) move faster, particles near the axis move slower, and a particle on the axis has v = 0.
Also, the direction of v (along the tangent) keeps changing, so even for one particle the linear velocity is not constant in direction; only its magnitude is constant when ω is constant.

blocks.prompt: 3.2 A loaf of bread is lying on rotating plate. A crow takes away the loaf of bread and the plates rotation increase. Why?
blocks.explanation:
This is due to the law of conservation of angular momentum.
When the crow lifts the loaf (no external torque about the axis), the mass on the plate decreases, so the moment of inertia of the rotating system decreases from I₁ to I₂.
Since I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂ and I₂ < I₁, the angular velocity ω₂ becomes greater than ω₁; so the plate rotates faster.

blocks.prompt: 3.3 Why do we tumble when we take the sharp turn with large speed?
blocks.explanation:
On a sharp turn (small r) at large speed the centripetal force needed, F = mv²/r, is very large.
Our feet are turned with the vehicle by friction, but the upper part of our body, due to inertia, tends to continue in a straight line (outward from the turn). The friction and our grip cannot supply this large centripetal force, so the body leans outward and we tumble.

blocks.prompt: 3.4 What will be time period of a simple pendulum in an artificial satellite?
blocks.explanation:
In an orbiting satellite everything is in a state of weightlessness, so the effective value of g inside it is zero.
T = 2π√(l/g) = 2π√(l/0) = infinite.
So the pendulum does not oscillate at all; its time period is infinite.

blocks.prompt: 3.5 Is the motion of a satellite in its orbit, uniform or accelerated?
blocks.explanation:
It is accelerated. The satellite moves in a (nearly) circular orbit with constant speed, but the direction of its velocity changes at every point.
The Earth's gravitational pull provides a centripetal acceleration a = v²/r (= g at that height) directed towards the centre of the Earth. So the motion is uniform in speed but accelerated.

blocks.prompt: 3.6 What are the advantages that radian has been preferred as SI unit over degree?
blocks.explanation:
1. A radian is the ratio of two lengths (θ = S/r), so it is a natural unit that does not depend on an arbitrary division of the circle (like 360°).
2. The simple relations S = rθ, v = rω and a = rα hold only when θ is in radians; in degrees extra conversion factors are needed.
3. It makes calculations of angular quantities and their relation with linear quantities simple and direct (1 rev = 2π rad, 1 rad = 57.3°).

blocks.prompt: 3.7 In uniform circular motion, what are the average velocity and average acceleration for one revolution? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Both are zero.
Average velocity = total displacement ÷ time. After one revolution the body returns to its starting point, so displacement = 0 and average velocity = 0.
Average acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = (v_f − v_i)/T. After one revolution the velocity has the same magnitude and the same direction as at the start, so v_f − v_i = 0 and average acceleration = 0.
(The instantaneous acceleration v²/r is not zero; only the average over a full revolution is zero.)

blocks.prompt: 3.8 In a rainstorm with a strong wind, what determines the best position to hold an umbrella?
blocks.explanation:
The direction of the resultant (relative) velocity of the rain determines it.
The rain drops have a vertical velocity v_r (falling) and the wind gives them a horizontal velocity v_w. Their resultant makes an angle θ with the vertical, where tan θ = v_w / v_r.
The umbrella should be tilted towards the wind so that its shaft is along this resultant direction of the rain (if we are walking, our own velocity is also included in the relative velocity of rain).

blocks.prompt: 3.9 A ball is just supported by a string without breaking. If it is whirled in a vertical circle, it breaks. Explain why.
blocks.explanation:
When the ball just hangs at rest, the tension is T = mg, and the string can just bear this.
When the ball is whirled in a vertical circle, at the lowest point the tension must support the weight and also provide the centripetal force:
T − mg = mv²/r, so T = mg + mv²/r.
This tension is greater than mg, i.e. more than the string can withstand, so the string breaks (usually near the lowest point).

blocks.prompt:
3.10 How the centripetal force supplied in the following cases:
(a) A satellite orbiting around the Earth.
(b) A car taking a turn on a level road.
(c) A stone whirled in a circle by means of a string.
blocks.explanation:
(a) The gravitational force of attraction between the Earth and the satellite provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r.
(b) The force of friction between the tyres and the level road provides the centripetal force.
(c) The tension in the string, pulling the stone towards the centre, provides the centripetal force.

blocks.prompt: 3.1 What is meant by angular momentum? Explain the law of conservation of angular momentum with daily life examples.
blocks.explanation:
Angular momentum:
A particle has angular momentum about an axis if its angular position changes relative to that axis. For a particle of mass m with momentum p = mv at position vector r from the origin O:
L = r × p
Magnitude: L = rp sin θ = mrv sin θ, where θ is the angle between r and p.
Direction: perpendicular to the plane of r and p, given by the right hand rule. SI unit: kg m² s⁻¹ (or J s).
For circular motion θ = 90°, so L = mrv = mr²ω; for a rigid body L = Iω.

Law of conservation of angular momentum:
If no external torque acts on a system, the total angular momentum of the system remains constant.
L_total = L₁ + L₂ + … = constant
For a single spinning body that changes its moment of inertia from I₁ to I₂: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂. If I decreases, ω increases, and vice versa. The direction of L (the axis of rotation) also stays fixed unless an external torque acts.

Daily life examples:
1. Diver: after leaving the board he curls his arms and legs in, I decreases, ω increases and he takes somersaults; before reaching the water he stretches out, I increases and ω decreases.
2. Ice skater: by folding the arms and bringing the stretched leg close, I decreases and he spins faster; stretching arms and leg out slows him down.
3. Person on a turntable with dumb-bells: drawing the hands inward decreases I and the angular speed at once increases.
4. Bicycle/bike: the angular momentum of the spinning wheels resists change and keeps the moving bike upright.
5. Earth's axis stays fixed in direction as it moves round the Sun (no sizeable torque), giving the seasons; melting polar ice flowing towards the equator increases the Earth's I and slightly decreases its angular velocity (longer day).

blocks.prompt: 3.2 Show that orbital angular momentum; L = Iω.
blocks.explanation:
Single particle:
A particle of mass m moves in a circle of radius r with angular velocity ω. Its momentum p = mv is along the tangent, so the angle between r and p is 90°.
L = rp sin 90° = mrv
But v = rω, hence L = mr²ω.
For a particle, mr² = I (its moment of inertia about the axis), so L = Iω.

Rigid body:
A symmetric rigid body rotates about a fixed axis through its centre of mass with angular velocity ω. It is made of particles m₁, m₂, …, mₙ at distances r₁, r₂, …, rₙ from the axis; each moves in a circle with the same ω.
Angular momentum of the iᵗʰ particle: Lᵢ = mᵢvᵢrᵢ = mᵢrᵢ²ω (as vᵢ = rᵢω), along the axis.
Total angular momentum:
L = m₁r₁²ω + m₂r₂²ω + … + mₙrₙ²ω = (Σ mᵢrᵢ²) ω
Since Σ mᵢrᵢ² = I, the moment of inertia of the body about the axis:
L = Iω (in vector form L⃗ = Iω⃗, along the axis of rotation).

blocks.prompt: 3.3 Define moment of inertia. Prove that torque acting on rotating rigid body is equal to the product of its moment of inertia and angular momentum.
blocks.explanation:
Moment of inertia:
The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is the sum of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis: I = Σ mᵢrᵢ². It plays the same role in rotational motion as mass in linear motion. Unit: kg m².

Proof (τ = Iα):
Single particle: a mass m at the end of a massless rod of length r, pivoted at O, is acted on by a force F perpendicular to the rod.
F = ma_T, and a_T = rα, so F = mrα.
Multiplying both sides by r: rF = mr²α, i.e. τ = mr²α.
Rigid body: the body is made of particles m₁, m₂, …, mₙ at distances r₁, r₂, …, rₙ from the axis. Torque on each: τ₁ = m₁r₁²α, τ₂ = m₂r₂²α, …, τₙ = mₙrₙ²α. Since the body is rigid, all particles have the same angular acceleration α.
τ_total = (m₁r₁² + m₂r₂² + … + mₙrₙ²) α = (Σ mᵢrᵢ²) α
τ = Iα
Thus the torque on a rotating rigid body equals the product of its moment of inertia and its angular acceleration (rotational form of F = ma).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "product of its moment of inertia and angular momentum". Torque equals the product of moment of inertia and angular acceleration (τ = Iα, Eq. 3.18); I × angular momentum is not a torque. The answer proves τ = Iα.

blocks.prompt: 3.4 What are artificial satellites? Calculate the minimum time period necessary to put a satellite into the orbit.
blocks.explanation:
Artificial satellites:
Satellites are objects that orbit in a nearly circular path around the Earth. Artificial satellites are man-made; they are put into orbit by rockets and held in orbit by the gravitational pull of the Earth, which provides the centripetal force. They are used for communication, weather forecasting, GPS navigation, etc.

Minimum period (satellite orbiting close to the Earth's surface):
For a low orbit, the centripetal acceleration is g: g = v²/R
v = √(gR) = √(9.8 m s⁻² × 6.4 × 10⁶ m) = 7.9 × 10³ m s⁻¹ = 7.9 km s⁻¹
This is the critical (minimum) velocity to put a satellite into orbit.
Time period: T = 2πR/v = 2π√(R/g)
T = 2 × 3.14 × 6.4 × 10⁶ m ÷ 7.9 × 10³ m s⁻¹
T ≈ 5.08 × 10³ s ≈ 85 min (the book quotes 5060 s ≈ 84 min)
A satellite placed higher needs a smaller speed and takes longer for one revolution, so this is the minimum period.

blocks.prompt: 3.5 Define orbital velocity. Derive an expression for the same.
blocks.explanation:
Orbital velocity:
The velocity with which a satellite revolves round the Earth in its orbit is called its orbital velocity.

Derivation:
Let a satellite of mass mₛ move with orbital speed v in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth of mass M.
The centripetal force required: F_c = mₛv²/r
This force is provided by the gravitational force: F_g = Gmₛ M/r²
Equating: Gmₛ M/r² = mₛv²/r
v² = GM/r
v = √(GM/r)   (Eq. 3.15)
The orbital velocity does not depend on the mass of the satellite; it depends only on the mass of the Earth and the radius of the orbit (a higher orbit needs a smaller speed).
Near the Earth's surface (r ≈ R, GM/R² = g): v = √(gR) = √(9.8 × 6.4 × 10⁶) ≈ 7.9 km s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 3.6 Write a note on artificial gravity. Derive an expression for frequency with which the spaceship rotates to provide artificial gravity.
blocks.explanation:
Artificial gravity:
In a gravity-free space (orbiting spaceship) nothing pushes a body to any side of the spacecraft. Over a long stay this weightlessness affects the health and performance of astronauts. To overcome this, the spaceship is rotated about its own axis. The outer wall (floor) then pushes on the astronauts and provides the centripetal force; they feel this push like weight. This gravity-like effect is called artificial gravity.

Derivation:
Let the outer radius of the spaceship be R and it rotates with angular speed ω. Centripetal acceleration of a point on the rim:
a_c = Rω²
ω = 2π/t (t = period of revolution), so a_c = R(2π)²/t² = 4π²R/t²
As f = 1/t: a_c = 4π²Rf²
f² = a_c/(4π²R), f = (1/2π)√(a_c/R)
For gravity like the Earth, a_c = g:
f = (1/2π)√(g/R)   (Eq. 3.17)
When the spaceship rotates with this frequency, the inhabitants feel artificial gravity equal to the Earth's gravity.

blocks.prompt: 3.7 Prove that; (i) v = rω and (ii) a = rα
blocks.explanation:
Consider a rigid body rotating about the z-axis. A point P is at perpendicular distance r from the axis; OP is the reference line.

(i) v = rω
In a short time Δt, P moves through an arc P₁P₂ = ΔS while OP turns through an angle Δθ (in radians). By S = rθ:
ΔS = r Δθ
Dividing by Δt: ΔS/Δt = r (Δθ/Δt)
In the limit Δt → 0, ΔS/Δt = v (linear speed of P, along the tangent) and Δθ/Δt = ω (angular velocity of OP):
v = rω   (Eq. 3.7)

(ii) a = rα
If the angular velocity changes from ωᵢ to ω_f in time Δt, the linear velocity changes from vᵢ = rωᵢ to v_f = rω_f:
Δv = v_f − vᵢ = r(ω_f − ωᵢ) = r Δω
Dividing by Δt: Δv/Δt = r (Δω/Δt)
In the limit Δt → 0, Δv/Δt = a_t (tangential acceleration) and Δω/Δt = α (angular acceleration):
a_t = rα   (Eq. 3.8)
These show that points at larger distance from the axis have larger linear speed and acceleration, while all have the same ω and α.

blocks.prompt: 3.1 A laser beam is directed from the Earth to the moon. The beam spreads over a diameter of 2.50 cm at the moon surface, What is divergence angle of the beam? The distance of moon from the Earth is 3.8 × 10⁸ m. (Ans: 6.6 × 10^? rad, exponent not legible in the print)
blocks.explanation:
Given: diameter of the spot on the moon S = 2.50 cm = 0.025 m; distance to the moon r = 3.8 × 10⁸ m
Required: divergence angle θ = ?
The spot is a very small arc of a circle of radius r, so S = rθ:
θ = S/r
θ = 0.025 m ÷ 3.8 × 10⁸ m
θ = 6.6 × 10⁻¹¹ rad

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The power of ten in the printed answer is not legible in the print. 0.025 m ÷ 3.8 × 10⁸ m = 6.58 × 10⁻¹¹ rad, so the answer is 6.6 × 10⁻¹¹ rad.

blocks.prompt: 3.2 A car is moving with a speed of 108 km h⁻¹. If its wheel has a diameter of 60 cm, find its angular speed in rad s⁻¹ and rev s⁻¹. (Ans: 100 rad s⁻¹, 16 rev s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: v = 108 km h⁻¹ = 108 × 1000 m ÷ 3600 s = 30 m s⁻¹
Diameter = 60 cm, so r = 30 cm = 0.30 m
Required: ω = ? (in rad s⁻¹ and rev s⁻¹)
v = rω, so ω = v/r
ω = 30 m s⁻¹ ÷ 0.30 m
ω = 100 rad s⁻¹
In rev s⁻¹ (1 rev = 2π rad):
f = ω/2π = 100 ÷ (2 × 3.14) = 15.9 rev s⁻¹ ≈ 16 rev s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 3.3 An electric motor is running at 1800 rev min⁻¹. On switching OFF it comes to rest in 20 s. If angular retardation is uniform, find the number of revolutions it makes before stopping. (Ans: 300 rev)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ωᵢ = 1800 rev min⁻¹ = 1800 ÷ 60 = 30 rev s⁻¹; ω_f = 0; t = 20 s
Required: number of revolutions θ = ?
α = (ω_f − ωᵢ)/t = (0 − 30 rev s⁻¹) ÷ 20 s = −1.5 rev s⁻²
θ = ωᵢt + ½αt²
θ = 30 rev s⁻¹ × 20 s + ½ × (−1.5 rev s⁻²) × (20 s)²
θ = 600 rev − 300 rev
θ = 300 rev
(Check: θ = average ω × t = (30 + 0)/2 × 20 = 300 rev.)

blocks.prompt: 3.4 A string 0.5 m long holding a stone can withstand maximum tension of 35.6 N. Find the maximum speed at which a stone of 0.5 kg can be whirled with it in a vertical circle. (Ans: 5.5 m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: r = 0.5 m; T_max = 35.6 N; m = 0.5 kg; g = 9.8 m s⁻²
Required: maximum speed v = ?
In a vertical circle the tension is maximum at the lowest point, where it supports the weight and provides the centripetal force:
T − mg = mv²/r, so T = mg + mv²/r
35.6 N = 0.5 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² + 0.5 kg × v² ÷ 0.5 m
35.6 = 4.9 + v²
v² = 30.7 m² s⁻²
v = 5.54 m s⁻¹ ≈ 5.5 m s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 3.5 The flywheel of an engine is rotating at 2100 rev min⁻¹ when the power source is shut off. What torque is required to stop it in 3 minutes? The moment of inertia of the flywheel is 36 kg m². (Ans: 44 N m)
blocks.explanation:
Given: ωᵢ = 2100 rev min⁻¹ = 2100 × 2π rad ÷ 60 s = 70π rad s⁻¹ = 219.9 rad s⁻¹; ω_f = 0
t = 3 min = 180 s; I = 36 kg m²
Required: torque τ = ?
α = (ω_f − ωᵢ)/t = (0 − 219.9 rad s⁻¹) ÷ 180 s = −1.22 rad s⁻²
τ = Iα
τ = 36 kg m² × 1.22 rad s⁻² (magnitude)
τ = 44 N m (acting opposite to the rotation)

blocks.prompt: 3.6 What is the moment of inertia of a 200 kg sphere whose diameter is 60 cm. (Ans: 28.8 kg m²)
blocks.explanation:
Given: M = 200 kg; diameter = 60 cm, so radius r = 30 cm = 0.30 m
Required: moment of inertia I = ?
For a solid sphere about a diameter (moments of inertia of various bodies, section 3.4: sphere of diameter 2r): I = (2/5) Mr²
I = 2/5 × 200 kg × (0.30 m)²
I = 0.4 × 200 × 0.09 kg m²
I = 7.2 kg m²

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints (Ans: 28.8 kg m²). That value comes from putting the diameter (0.60 m) in place of the radius: 2/5 × 200 × (0.60)² = 28.8. The chapter's formula I = (2/5)Mr² uses the radius r = 0.30 m, so I = 7.2 kg m².

blocks.prompt: 3.7 A satellite is orbiting the Earth at an altitude of 200 km. Assuming the Earth's radius is 6400 km, calculate the orbital speed of the satellite. (Ans: 7.78 km h⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: h = 200 km; R = 6400 km
Radius of orbit r = R + h = 6600 km = 6.6 × 10⁶ m
G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²; mass of the Earth M = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg
Required: orbital speed v = ?
v = √(GM/r)   (Eq. 3.15)
v = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.0 × 10²⁴ ÷ 6.6 × 10⁶) m s⁻¹
v = √(6.06 × 10⁷) m s⁻¹
v = 7.79 × 10³ m s⁻¹ ≈ 7.8 km s⁻¹ (7.78 km s⁻¹ with slightly different rounding of G and M)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the answer as 7.78 km h⁻¹. The number is right but the unit is wrong: the orbital speed is 7.78 km s⁻¹ (kilometres per second), about 28 000 km h⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 3.8 A space station has a radius of 20 m and rotates at an angular velocity of 0.5 rad s⁻¹. What is the artificial gravity experienced by the astronauts on the space station. (Ans: 5 m s⁻²)
blocks.explanation:
Given: R = 20 m; ω = 0.5 rad s⁻¹
Required: artificial gravity a_c = ?
a_c = Rω²
a_c = 20 m × (0.5 rad s⁻¹)²
a_c = 20 × 0.25 m s⁻²
a_c = 5 m s⁻² (about half of g)

blocks.prompt: 3.9 A bicycle wheel has an angular momentum of 10 kg m² s⁻¹ and angular velocity of 2 rad s⁻¹. Find the value of its moment of inertial. (Ans: 5 kg m²)
blocks.explanation:
Given: L = 10 kg m² s⁻¹; ω = 2 rad s⁻¹
Required: I = ?
L = Iω, so I = L/ω
I = 10 kg m² s⁻¹ ÷ 2 rad s⁻¹
I = 5 kg m²

blocks.prompt: 3.10 A diver comes off a board with arms straight up and legs straight down, giving him a moment of inertia of 18 kg m² about his rotation axis. Then tucks into a small ball, decreasing his moment of inertia to 3.6 kg m². While tucked, he makes two complete rotations in 1.0 second. If he had not tucked at all, how many revolutions would he have made in 1.5 s from board to water? (Ans: 0.6 rev)
blocks.explanation:
Given: I₁ (straight) = 18 kg m²; I₂ (tucked) = 3.6 kg m²
ω₂ (tucked) = 2 rev ÷ 1.0 s = 2 rev s⁻¹; t = 1.5 s
Required: revolutions in 1.5 s without tucking = ?
By conservation of angular momentum: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂
